title: America's Doctors Are About to Learn About Food for the First Time. Here Is Why NRI Patients Should Care.
excerpt: Seventy-three medical schools have pledged 40 hours of nutrition training. Licensing exams will test it. For South Asian patients whose food traditions were routinely dismissed, this is a watershed.
body:
For decades, the running joke in medicine has been that doctors know less about food than their patients do. The numbers have always backed it up: American medical students received an average of 1.2 hours of formal nutrition education per year. Only 14 per cent of residency programmes required any nutrition curriculum at all. Just 14 per cent of practising physicians felt comfortable discussing diet with their patients.

That era is ending. On June 8, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced that 73 medical schools — nearly half of all institutions in the country — have now signed a voluntary pledge to require at least 40 hours of nutrition education for students starting this autumn. Eight leading accrediting bodies, including the National Board of Medical Examiners, committed to embedding nutrition into licensing exams for the first time.

## What Actually Changed

The shift has three layers, each more consequential than the last.

First, the curriculum pledge. Medical schools including the University of Maryland, University of Massachusetts, Florida Atlantic University, and Texas A&M are among the 19 newest signatories, joining 54 schools that signed earlier in 2026. Students will need to demonstrate competency across 71 areas, ranging from understanding the nutritional differences between minimally processed and ultraprocessed foods to the responsible use of AI for dietary advice.

Second, the licensing exams. The National Board of Medical Examiners announced that approximately 15 per cent of content across its examination sequence will now assess nutrition knowledge and its clinical applications. The National Board of Osteopathic Medical Examiners made a comparable commitment. This means a medical student who skips nutrition coursework will not just miss out on knowledge — they will fail their boards.

Third, the funding. HHS launched a $2.1 million NIH challenge grant, the first phase of a planned $5 million initiative, to identify and scale effective approaches for integrating nutrition into medical and nursing school curricula. Winning programmes will be made publicly available.

“Poor diets are the primary driver of America’s chronic disease epidemic,” HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said at the announcement. “Education drives practice, practice drives outcomes, and outcomes determine the health of a nation.”

## The Scale of the Problem

The backdrop is staggering. Chronic disease and mental health expenditures cost the United States $4.4 trillion annually. An estimated one million Americans die each year from food-related chronic illnesses. Yet the physicians treating them have historically been trained to reach for a prescription pad, not a conversation about what their patients eat for breakfast.

Dr. Mehmet Oz, now administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid, put it bluntly: “If we don’t learn these things in medical school, they cannot be important, because everything we learn that’s important about health, we’re going to learn in medical school. The arrogance that’s associated with not learning about nutrition in medical school contaminates the entire medical space.”

Twenty-four states have also tied Rural Health Transformation Fund allocations to requiring nutrition education as part of continuing medical education credits, creating a financial incentive for practising physicians to catch up with what their newer colleagues will learn from the start.

## Why the Diaspora Should Pay Attention

For Indian Americans, this shift carries a particular resonance. South Asian patients have long navigated a disconnect between their own food traditions — the turmeric in dal, the fermented dosa batter, the use of specific spices for specific ailments — and a medical establishment that often dismissed these practices as anecdotal. Many NRIs have described the frustration of a physician who could name every statin on the market but could not explain why the fibre in whole moong dal might matter for glycaemic control.

The new curriculum explicitly includes training on the health effects of minimally processed versus ultraprocessed foods, a distinction that South Asian cooking has implicitly understood for centuries. It also addresses cultural dietary patterns, meaning future physicians may be better equipped to counsel a patient whose diet centres on roti, rice, and sabzi rather than the standard Western food pyramid.

For the 5.4 million Indian Americans in the United States, many of whom face elevated risks of heart disease, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome, having a physician who understands the nutritional logic of their home kitchen is not a luxury. It is a clinical necessity. This generation of medical students may be the first equipped to deliver it.
